panels.body_site: dorsal hand and extensor surfaces of the fingers
panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a human hand showing erythematous papules and macular erythema over the dorsal MCP and interphalangeal joints, captioned as Gottron papules and Gottron sign, classic cutaneous manifestations of dermatomyositis.
panels.attribution_text: Kutwin et al. The Spectrum of Cutaneous Manifestations in Dermatomyositis: A Comprehensive Review.. Journal of clinical medicine 2026. doi:10.3390/jcm15082874. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Gottron’s papules and Gottron’s sign.
in_text_mentions: olaceous, slightly elevated papular lesions arising on an erythematous base. They are typically located on extensor surfaces overlying bony prominences, particularly the metacarpophalangeal and proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, and may extend to involve the periungual regions [25,26] (Figure 1 and Figure 2). Gottron’s sign refers to flat erythematous macules, often arranged linearly, affecting the dorsal and lateral parts of the hands and fingers. These lesions frequently undergo subsequent scaling and may also be observed on other extensor sites, including the elbows and knees [25].

Due to these symptoms, she had blood work that showed a positive rheumatoid factor (RF), positive anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody, and mildly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). She became more alarmed when she noted bumps on her knuckles, some with overlying ulcers despite no history of trauma (Fig. 1).Fig. 1Gottron's papules with overlying ulcers are highly specific for MDA-5 dermatomyositis. o support this diagnosis. Gottron's papules are one of the most characteristic findings of DM, manifesting as erythematous to violaceous papules and/or plaques with or without scale over the bilateral metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and/or distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints (Fig. 1). Occasionally, Gottron's papules can involve the sides of the fingers and the interphalangeal skin. Stretch is believed to play a role in the pathophysiology of Gottron's papules, which is why they can be more prominent on or isolated to a patient's dominant hand (Kurtzman et al., 2016).

Physical examination revealed a tall, thin woman in no acute distress. Her cutaneous exam is shown in Figs. 1-2. Her lungs had diffuse, dry crackles most notable in the bases. Musculoskeletal examination was notable for synovitis across the MCP and PIP joints. The strength in her neck flexors as well as proximal and distal upper and lower extremities was normal.

in_text_mentions: papules are highly concerning for a subtype of DM associated with the anti-melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) autoantibody. These ulcers, along with painful palmar macules and papules (Fig. 3, Fig. 4), are highly specific for this phenotype, which confers a higher risk of interstitial lung disease (ILD) (Kurtzman and Vleugels, 2018). Because the autoantibodies for DM can take months to return, in almost all cases, DM should be considered a clinical diagnosis based on physical exam, with work-up and monitoring guided by the patient's findings. in_text_mentions: ially skin lesions, such as periorbital blue-purple rash, reddish rash on the face, anterior chest (V-sign), and shoulders (shawl sign), and a violaceous eruption on the knuckles (Gottron’s papules), which are characteristics of dermatomyositis (Figure 1)3. Pulmonary complications, due to interstitial lung disease, may occur in 10 to 40% of patients, as well as fever, arthralgia, scleroderma, and Raynaud’s phenomenon, mainly in overlap and antisynthetase syndrome, defined as the presence of myopathy, fever, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud’s phenomenon, arthritis, and “mechanic’s hands” 10 .

is a condition seen in adults and children, mainly females, characterized by cutaneous manifestations and proximal muscle weakness. Presentation includes generalized erythema, mainly in the upper region of the trunk (shawl or V sign), purplish lesion around the eyes (heliotrope), and violet eruptions on the finger joints (Gottron’s sign), all of which are photosensitive (Figure 1) 16 . Some patients develop an interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon and calcifications in muscles or skin, although the trend is to categorize them separately if an ASS-specific autoantibody is recognized 5 .

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Patient-derived dermatomyositis muscle biopsy with characteristic perifascicular atrophy on HES staining. B: Patient-derived dermatomyositis muscle biopsy showing perivascular/perimysial inflammatory infiltrates and nuclear internalisations. C: Higher-power HES image from the dermatomyositis biopsy demonstrating inflammatory inflammation around muscle vessels and connective tissue. D: C5b9 immunohistochemistry from the dermatomyositis biopsy demonstrates membrane attack complex deposition around myofibers. E: Patient-derived MHC-1 immunostain shows the diffuse membrane pattern with perifascicular enhancement described as typical of dermatomyositis. F: CD4 immunohistochemistry from the dermatomyositis muscle biopsy demonstrates perivascular and endomysial lymphocytic infiltration.

panels.figure_caption: Muscle biopsy of patient #3. Representative images of patient #3's muscle biopsy, performed at the time of IIM diagnosis, showing histological features typical of dermatomyositis. A, B, C, Hematoxylin-Eosin-Safran (HES) staining (A, B: 20×; C: 40×), showing perifascicular atrophic fibers (A), perivascular and perimysial inflammation (B, C), and nuclear internalisations (B). D, Terminal complement membrane attack complex (C5b9) staining (63×), showing membrane deposition around several fibers. E, Major histocompatibility complex type 1 (MHC 1) staining (20×), showing diffuse membrane positivity with perifascicular enhancement. F, CD4 staining (20×), showing perivascular and endomysial CD4+ T-cell infiltrates (Dr Diane Giovannini, Département d’Anatomie et de Cytologie Pathologiques-IBP, CHU de Grenoble, France).
in_text_mentions: ents: Gottron papules (2/3), heliotrope rash (2/3), psoriasiform plaques (3/3), and manicure sign (1/3). Signs of peripheral microangiopathy were present in patients #2 (giant capillaries) and #3 (Raynaud phenomenon and dystrophic capillaries); nailfold capillaroscopy was normal in patient #1. Muscle involvement was variable: inexistent in patient #2, moderate (muscle pain without weakness) in patient #3, and severe (muscle weakness, swallowing difficulties and increased CPK levels) in patient #1. In myopathic patients, muscle involvement was confirmed by EMG and muscle biopsy (Figs. 2 and 3).

panels.rationale: The caption directly identifies calcinosis cutis, and the dermatomyositis-focused article specifically discusses this manifestation in DM. The photograph visibly shows clustered inflamed nodules with pale calcific material. No DM subtype or patient ethnicity is explicitly established for this panel.
panels.attribution_text: Kutwin et al. The Spectrum of Cutaneous Manifestations in Dermatomyositis: A Comprehensive Review.. Journal of clinical medicine 2026. doi:10.3390/jcm15082874. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 13.
panels.figure_caption: Calcinosis cutis.
in_text_mentions: laris, and mucosal or digital ulcerations. In adults, vasculitic skin changes have been associated with underlying malignancy [27]. Calcinosis cutis is characterized by calcium deposition within the skin and subcutaneous tissues, forming firm nodules most often located on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. While it affects up to 70% of patients with JDM, it occurs in approximately 10% of adults with DM [33]. Extrusion of calcium deposits may result in chronic, non-healing ulcers [27]. In adults, calcinosis has been linked to both solid and hematologic malignancies [33] (Figure 12 and Figure 13).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: The human skeletal-muscle H&E biopsy directly demonstrates perifascicular atrophy, a characteristic histopathologic manifestation of classic dermatomyositis. B: The captioned muscle biopsy shows a contiguous area of necrotic myofibers corresponding to a microinfarct, a recognized histopathologic lesion in dermatomyositis. C: The H&E panel directly demonstrates punch-out vacuoles within myofibers, captioned as focal myosinolysis in dermatomyositis. D: HLA-ABC immunostaining directly shows widespread myofiber MHC-class I expression with perifascicular reinforcement, a characteristic immunopathologic feature of dermatomyositis. E: CD56/NCAM immunostaining demonstrates extensive positive myofibers, which the caption identifies as indicating muscle ischemia in dermatomyositis. F: PECAM/CD31 immunostaining highlights endomysial vessels and demonstrates marked capillary dropout, corresponding to the characteristic microangiopathy of...

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial chest CT from a patient in the dermatomyositis-associated ILD article demonstrates the captioned fibrotic NSIP pattern, with subpleural ground-glass opacity, fine reticulation, and traction bronchiectasis. B: Axial chest CT shows the captioned fibrotic NSIP manifestation associated with dermatomyositis; arrows and arrowheads explicitly mark the ground-glass, reticular, and traction-bronchiectatic abnormalities.
panels.attribution_text: Palmucci et al. Clinical and Radiological Features of Interstitial Lung Diseases Associated with Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis.. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania) 2022. doi:10.3390/medicina58121757. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern: patchy ground-glass opacities with a predominantly subpleural distribution (black arrow), fine reticulations (white arrow), and traction bronchiectasis (arrowheads).
in_text_mentions: The NSIP pattern is mainly represented by two main subtypes: fibrotic type and cellular type, the latter with a better prognosis due to a successful treatment response. On HRCT, the most common findings are ground-glass and fine reticulations (Figure 5 and Figure 6), predominantly in the lower lung zone with subpleural sparing. Generally, these abnormalities have symmetrical and bilateral localization with an apicobasal gradient.

Other manifestations include traction bronchiectasis (Figure 6 and Figure 7) and thickening of bronchovascular bundles—mostly associated with fibrotic NSIP or UIP/probable UIP— as well as lung volume loss, especially at the lower lobes [38]. In advanced disease, traction bronchiectasis, consolidations, and areas of microcystic honeycombing are often recognized. In some NSIP cases, HRCT may demonstrate peripheral areas of consolidations, also with perilobular appearance; in these cases, a mixed NSIP-OP pattern (Figure 8) may be revealed at imaging [39].

findings.label: Perifascicular atrophy
findings.evidence: Caption: showing endomysial inflammation, with mild perifascicular atrophy (A).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Patient #1's HES-stained muscle biopsy shows mild perifascicular atrophy, a characteristic histopathologic manifestation of dermatomyositis. B: HES-stained muscle tissue from patient #1 demonstrates perivascular inflammatory infiltration compatible with dermatomyositis. C: Higher-magnification HES image of patient #1's muscle biopsy shows dense perivascular inflammation characteristic of dermatomyositis. D: C5b9 immunostaining demonstrates capillary membrane attack complex deposition in a muscle biopsy classified as compatible with dermatomyositis. E: The caption identifies diffuse membrane positivity for MHC class I in patient #1's dermatomyositis muscle biopsy; this specific finding is not separately represented in the supplied vocabulary. F: CD3 immunostaining in patient #1's muscle biopsy shows a predominant T-cell inflammatory infiltrate, supporting the captioned dermatomyositis attribution.

panels.figure_caption: Muscle biopsy of patient #1. Representative images of patient #1's muscle biopsy, performed at the time of IIM diagnosis, showing histological features compatible with dermatomyositis. A, B, C, Hematoxylin-Erythrosin-Saffron (HES) staining (A, B: 20×; C: 40×), showing endomysial (A) and perivascular (B, C) inflammation, with mild perifascicular atrophy (A). D, Terminal complement membrane attack complex (C5b9) staining (40×), showing mild capillary C5b9 deposition. E, Major histocompatibility complex type 1 (MHC 1) staining (10×), showing diffuse membrane positivity. F, CD3 staining (40×), showing predominant T-cell inflammation (Claude-Alain Maurage, Université de Lille, F-59000 Lille, France).
in_text_mentions: ents: Gottron papules (2/3), heliotrope rash (2/3), psoriasiform plaques (3/3), and manicure sign (1/3). Signs of peripheral microangiopathy were present in patients #2 (giant capillaries) and #3 (Raynaud phenomenon and dystrophic capillaries); nailfold capillaroscopy was normal in patient #1. Muscle involvement was variable: inexistent in patient #2, moderate (muscle pain without weakness) in patient #3, and severe (muscle weakness, swallowing difficulties and increased CPK levels) in patient #1. In myopathic patients, muscle involvement was confirmed by EMG and muscle biopsy (Figs. 2 and 3).

findings.evidence: Caption: Heliotrope rash with periorbital edema.

panels.rationale: A single, clear clinical photograph shows symmetric violaceous upper-eyelid erythema with periorbital edema, the captioned heliotrope rash, a classic cutaneous manifestation of dermatomyositis.
panels.attribution_text: Kutwin et al. The Spectrum of Cutaneous Manifestations in Dermatomyositis: A Comprehensive Review.. Journal of clinical medicine 2026. doi:10.3390/jcm15082874. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Heliotrope rash with periorbital edema.
in_text_mentions: s include heliotrope rash, shawl sign, V-sign, nailfold abnormalities (Keining’s sign), and scalp dermatitis [27]. Heliotrope rash is characterized by symmetrical violaceous erythema, at times with accompanying oedema, predominantly affecting the upper eyelids and often associated with pruritus. Extension to the cheeks, nasal bridge, and nasolabial folds may occur. In some individuals, the presentation is limited to subtle eyelid discoloration or dilated eyelids vessels. Patients with lupus erythematosus (LE) and scleroderma may also rarely present heliotrope rash [28] (Figure 3 and Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: The NSIP pattern is mainly represented by two main subtypes: fibrotic type and cellular type, the latter with a better prognosis due to a successful treatment response. On HRCT, the most common findings are ground-glass and fine reticulations (Figure 5 and Figure 6), predominantly in the lower lung zone with subpleural sparing. Generally, these abnormalities have symmetrical and bilateral localization with an apicobasal gradient.

(a) HRCT at onset disease shows irregular linear opacities, subpleural reticulation, and consolidation. (b) HRCT taken 12 months later shows increase of subpleural reticulations. (c) HRCT taken 24 months later shows further increase of the interstitial involvement with ground-glass opacities.
in_text_mentions: n HRCT scans, the most common encountered lesions were GGOs (98.4%), followed by reticular opacities (67.2%) and consolidations (48.4%); the distribution of lesions was homogeneous, mainly represented in the lower lung lobes (98.4%), around the bronchovascular bundles (73.4%), and in the periphery (95.3%) (Figure 12); it may be also accompanied by a loss of volume [56]. Hozumi et al. confirmed these findings, reporting that all CT findings—in patients positive for anti-ARS Abs—were associated with NSIP pattern or NSIP with OP pattern [46]. Similar findings were also found in other series [59].

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: "Clinical presentation of erythematous papules and plaques over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron’s papules)."

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of a real hand showing erythematous papules and plaques over the MCP and interphalangeal joints, explicitly captioned as Gottron papules in a dermatomyositis study. B: Videodermoscopic patient image of Gottron papules in a dermatomyositis-focused article; colored arrowheads and arrows identify the captioned vessel patterns and white structureless areas. C: Videodermoscopic patient image explicitly identified as showing Gottron papules, with arrows and arrowheads indicating dotted vessels and irregular pink structureless areas.
panels.attribution_text: Żychowska and Reich. Dermoscopy and Trichoscopy in Dermatomyositis-A Cross-Sectional Study.. Journal of clinical medicine 2022. doi:10.3390/jcm11020375. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Clinical presentation of erythematous papules and plaques over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron’s papules). (b) Videodermoscopy of Gottron’s papules showed irregularly distributed dotted (black arrowhead), linear vessels with branches (blue arrowhead), and linear curved vessels (yellow arrowhead) surrounding white structureless areas (black arrow). (c) Videodermoscopy of Gottron’s papules showing predominantly dotted vessels (black arrowhead) surrounding irregular pink structureless areas (black arrow).
in_text_mentions: r vessels, linear vessels with branches, and linear curved vessels were noted in 53.9%, 46.2%, and 30.8% of cases, respectively. At least two vessel morphologies (i.e., pleomorphic vessels) were present in 76.9% of patients. The vessels were arranged irregularly in an unspecified pattern (100%). White scaling was predominantly (76.9%) observed and showed a patchy arrangement in the majority of cases (69.2%). Pink (76.9%) or white (46.2%) structureless areas were frequent findings. Follicular plugs or red hemorrhagic dots were observed less commonly (each in 38.5% of cases) (Table 4, Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: Capillaroscopy (dermoscopy of the nailfolds) was performed in all patients (n = 15). Four patients did not show any abnormalities in nailfold capillaroscopy. In the remaining group, the most frequent findings were elongated capillaries (90.9%), followed by avascular areas (81.8%), disorganized vessel architecture (81.8%), tortuous capillaries (72.7%), dilated capillaries (72.7%), and hemorrhages (72.7%). “Bushy” capillaries and giant capillaries were observed less frequently, in 45.5% and 36.4% of cases, respectively (Table 2, Figure 1).

Annals of the rheumatic diseases 2015. doi:10.1136/annrheumdis-2013-203396. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Features of dermatomyositis including the informative score tool items selected for the modified score tool, illustrated in a quadriceps biopsy (A, C, D, F and H) and in a biceps biopsy (B, E, G and I). Perivascular inflammation was seen, often with a perimysial localisation (A and B, arrows indicate vessels). Perifascicular fibre atrophy was a feature of some biopsies, and other fibre abnormalities including basophilia, indicating regeneration, were often more prominent in perifascicular regions (B, double arrow). CD3 immunoreactive T cells were present in the perimysium (C and E, arrows) and also the endomysium (D, arrow). Macrophage infiltrates were identified by CD68 immunohistochemistry in the endomysium (F and G, arrow) and also around vessels (G, double arrow). Neonatal myosin expression could often be seen to have a characteristic perifascicular pattern (H and I). (A and B) haematoxylin and eosin; (C, D and E) CD3 immunohistochemistry; (F and G) CD68 immunohistochemistry; (H and I) neonatal myosin immunohistochemistry. Bars represent: 50 µm in A, B, C, E and G; 25 µm in D and F; 100 µm in H; 260 µm in I.
in_text_mentions: e, overexpression of MHC protein on muscle fibres and infarction, had an α score of 0 indicating high agreement, but low variability since they were either always abnormal (MHC overexpression) or very rarely seen (infarction). These items were excluded from the modified score tool. Selection of an element for further analysis depended on the performance of that element rather than the importance of the pathological feature for diagnostic purposes. Representative examples of items selected for inclusion in the modified score tool, from both biceps and quadriceps biopsies, are shown in figure 1.

C: Clinical photograph of the anterior neck and upper chest with caption-confirmed V-sign distribution erythema and dyspigmented or hypopigmented plaques in the same dermatomyositis patient. panels.figure_caption: The cutaneous biopsy of flagellate erythema (magnification ×10) depicting atrophic epiderma. In the superficial derma, there was a slight inflammatory infiltrate, essentially composed of mononuclear cells and rare telangiectasies.
in_text_mentions: led bilateral basal pulmonary infiltrates that were confirmed by a high-resolution computed chest tomography. Pulmonary function tests were performed and showed significantly reduced DLCO compatible with interstitial lung disease. A cutaneous biopsy of the flagellate erythema was done and histological analysis was compatible with a diagnosis of dermatomyositis (Figure 2). Treatment with Methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg daily improved the dermatological features and the liver tests but the muscular pain did not subside. AZA (2 mg/kg/d) was then added but the patient's condition still did not improve.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Real human HRCT from the captioned 49-year-old anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis patient with DM-ILD and RP-ILD; the mild pulmonary findings are explicitly described in the caption. b: Real human HRCT from the captioned 43-year-old anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis patient with DM-ILD and RP-ILD; marked interstitial pulmonary fibrosis is explicitly described. c: Real human HRCT from the captioned 27-year-old anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis patient with DM-ILD. panels.figure_caption: HRCT findings in anti-MDA5 + DM-ILD patients with or without RP-ILD in the external validation dataset. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photograph from the reported patient shows erythema nodosum-like lesions on the right arm and forearm. The in-text report identifies these lesions as a panniculitis manifestation of dermatomyositis. B: H&E-stained lesional biopsy shows inflammatory cells involving adipose lobules and surrounding adipocytes, with a captioned perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. The disease-focused article attributes this panniculitis to dermatomyositis. C: H&E-stained tissue from the reported patient's lesional skin demonstrates dermoepidermal inflammation with focal epidermal infiltration. It is presented as part of the dermatomyositis-associated panniculitis evaluation. D: H&E-stained lesional dermis shows peri-adnexal and perivascular inflammation with foci of lymphocytic vasculitis in the case of refractory dermatomyositis-associated panniculitis.

findings.label: Rapidly progressive ILD
findings.evidence: The caption identifies the lung as being from a DM patient with RP-ILD.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Patient-derived lung-tissue immunohistochemistry from a dermatomyositis patient with chronic interstitial lung disease. The boxed region and arrow identify adrenomedullin staining, described as weak in macrophages and alveolar epithelial cells. B: Higher-magnification lung immunohistochemistry from the dermatomyositis patient with chronic ILD, showing adrenomedullin-positive cells corresponding to the boxed region in panel A. C: Patient-derived lung-tissue immunohistochemistry from a dermatomyositis patient with rapidly progressive ILD. The boxed area highlights stronger adrenomedullin staining. D: Higher-magnification lung immunohistochemistry corresponding to panel C, with arrows indicating strong adrenomedullin staining in macrophages and alveolar epithelial cells from a dermatomyositis patient with RP-ILD.
panels.attribution_text: Ye et al. Adrenomedullin Expression Is Associated With the Severity and Poor Prognosis of Interstitial Lung Disease in Dermatomyositis Patients.. Frontiers in immunology 2022. doi:10.3389/fimmu.2022.885142. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Enhanced adrenomedullin expression in the lung tissue of DM patients with RP-ILD. (A, B) The lung of a DM patient with chronic ILD. Positive adrenomedullin staining was detected in macrophages (black arrowhead) and alveolar epithelial cells (white arrowhead). (C, D) The lung of a DM patient with RP-ILD. Positive adrenomedullin staining was detected in macrophages (black arrowhead) and alveolar epithelial cells (white arrowhead). Scale bar = 50 μm. DM, dermatomyositis; ILD, interstitial lung disease; RP-ILD, rapidly progressive ILD.
in_text_mentions: To investigate the cellular location and the source of adrenomedullin in the lungs, we performed immunohistochemical staining for adrenomedullin from two patients with DM patients with ILD. Sections from DM patients with chronic ILD exhibited weak staining for adrenomedullin in macrophages and alveolar epithelial cells ( Figures 4A, B ), whereas those from DM patients with RP-ILD were strongly positive for adrenomedullin in macrophages and alveolar epithelial cells ( Figures 4C, D ).

in_text_mentions: In our cohort, 16 patients (19%) demonstrated positive staining for anti-MxA antibodies in their myofibres, with the staining patterns observed either in the sarcoplasm (10 cases) or the sarcolemma (six cases). Notably, all the patients with sarcoplasmic MxA expression were from the IIM group, while sarcolemmal MxA positivity was predominantly seen in the HMD group (five cases), p = 0.001 (Table 3). Additionally, one anti-MDA5-positive DM patient displayed this unique pattern in the perifascicular region (Figure 1F).

On the conventional light microscopy, all the IIM patients showed clear inflammatory cell infiltrate as well as necrosis and regeneration of muscle fibres. We observed variable patterns depending on the IIM subtype: non-specific myogenic changes in OM, perivascular inflammatory infiltrate with PFA in DM, severe atrophy with nuclear inclusions and rimmed vacuoles in IBM, fibrosis and vasculopathy in scleromyositis, perifascicular necrosis and inflammation in ASyS, and diffuse necrotizing myopathy with moderate inflammatory infiltrate in IMNM (Figure 1A–F).

the perifascicular area. MxA was detected even in some DM patients without PFA. By contrast, anti-MDA5 antibody-positive DM had the lowest relative sensitivity of MxA expression. In our three anti-MDA5-positive DM patients, the first 42-year-old patient had significant proximal muscle weakness, typical skin lesions and ILD with normal CK levels, and had no MxA expression on their myofibres. The second patient showed only sarcolemmal immunoreactivity in the myofibres of the perifascicular area, and the third one had a mild and scattered distribution pattern of MxA-positive fibres (Figure 1A–F).

in_text_mentions: companied by periorbital edema, commonly referred to as heliotrope rash. An erythematous rash was also observed on the extensor surfaces of joints, including the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles, indicative of the Gottron sign. Rashes were also present over sun-exposed regions, specifically the anterior neck and chest, forming a V-shaped pattern, commonly known as V-sign. The rashes were also present on the lateral aspect of the thigh, referred to as the holster sign, as shown in Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4. in_text_mentions: A 79-year-old male with a history of previous vocal cord carcinoma, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and atrial fibrillation presented to the emergency department with a six-week history of extreme fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, and characteristic skin rashes, including a heliotrope rash, Gottron papules (Figure 1), and a shawl sign. panels.rationale: Single human skeletal-muscle H&E image showing perifascicular atrophy, a characteristic histopathologic manifestation of dermatomyositis, with associated inflammatory infiltrate and myocyte necrosis.
panels.attribution_text: Ruiz Barrera et al. Intensive Care Management of Anti-Mi2-Positive Dermatomyositis: Lupus Overlap Syndrome.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.104509. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Predominantly perifascicular muscle fiber atrophy associated with an inflammatory infiltrate composed of lymphocytes and macrophages, as well as myocyte necrosis Hematoxylin and eosin stain; bright-field light microscopy. Total magnification ×100.
in_text_mentions: rformed, providing definitive diagnostic confirmation. Histopathologic examination revealed predominant perifascicular muscle fiber atrophy, a hallmark feature of dermatomyositis, associated with inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and macrophages, as well as focal myocyte necrosis (Figure 3). These findings reflect immune-mediated microvascular injury and perifascicular ischemic stress. At higher magnification, necrotic myocytes surrounded by inflammatory cells were clearly identified (Figure 4), confirming active muscle fiber destruction rather than a chronic or burnout process.

There were erythematous lesions with follicular hyperkeratosis and peripheral hyperpigmentation in the jaw area to the auricles, mimicking discoid lupus (Figure 1a).

There was myofiber necrosis, perifascicular atrophy [Figure 2] and patchy endomysial infiltrate of lymphocytes. Occasional endomysial capillaries showed deposits of membrane attack complex of complement. The morphologic features were consistent with DM.

panels.rationale: Patient-derived H&E muscle biopsy showing perifascicular atrophy and perivascular/perimysial chronic inflammation, characteristic histopathologic manifestations of juvenile dermatomyositis.

in_text_mentions: process; therefore, a muscle biopsy was performed. Deltoid muscle biopsy was performed, and the specimen was sent to be frozen in Isopentane cooled in liquid nitrogen. A panel of histology and histochemistry studies revealed a perifascicular atrophy pattern with the presence of atrophic basophilic degenerative/regenerative fibers at the periphery of the fascicles containing internalized nuclei (Figure 1a). in_text_mentions: Immunohistochemical analysis allowed further characterization of the inflammatory milieu and provided insight into the underlying immunopathogenesis. Abundant CD4⁺ T lymphocytes were observed between muscle fibers (Figure 5), indicating a prominent cell-mediated immune response consistent with T-cell-driven muscle injury. In parallel, CD20⁺ B lymphocytes showed a predominantly perivascular distribution (Figure 6), supporting the contribution of humoral immunity and autoantibody-mediated mechanisms, which are particularly relevant in dermatomyositis and overlap syndromes with SLE.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Human skeletal-muscle H&E from the reported cancer-associated dermatomyositis case shows perifascicular atrophy, a characteristic histopathologic manifestation of dermatomyositis. B: Human muscle H&E demonstrates perivascular inflammatory cuffing, a characteristic inflammatory histopathologic feature of dermatomyositis in this cancer-associated case. C: Muscle immunohistochemistry shows perifascicular MxA expression, a recognized type-I-interferon histopathologic marker supporting dermatomyositis in the reported cancer-associated case. D: Human skin H&E from the cancer-associated dermatomyositis case shows characteristic cutaneous histopathologic changes, including superficial vascular inflammation, epidermal atrophy, basal-cell hydropic degeneration, and dermal mucin. Skin tone cannot be assessed from histology.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: The caption specifically identifies left-arm papules and plaques, and the in-text description ties this eruption to anti-NXP-2 dermatomyositis in a disease-focused case report. The morphology is not specific enough to assign a standard dermatomyositis finding, so it is recorded in proposed_findings. B: This patient H&E biopsy is from the same dermatomyositis-associated left-arm eruption. The captioned superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate supports perivascular inflammation, while the interface, mucin, pigment-dropout, and eosinophil findings are retained as proposed findings; the vacuolar interface is circled.

(B) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain, 20× magnification. Site: arm. There is a subtle vacuolar interface (circled) with focal pigment dropout, a superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and increased dermal mucin.
in_text_mentions: an outside diagnosis of dermatomyositis with anti-NXP-2 positivity presented with pruritic and progressive papules and plaques on the upper and lower back (Figure 1A) and bilateral upper extremities (Figure 2A). Prior to presentation, an outside autoimmune work-up had been performed that was positive for ANA 1:160 in a speckled pattern and anti-NXP-2. ESR, CRP, Aldolase, and antibodies for beta 2 gylycoprotein, lupus anticoagulant, RNP, Smith, SmRNP, SSA, SSB, Scl70, Jo1, Centromere B, Chromatin, Ribosomal P, and anti-cardiolipin were negative. Anti-double-stranded DNA was equivocal. Two prior

cally, it was favored to represent a drug eruption, although clinically, the patient had not been placed on any new medications. A CBC was unremarkable for peripheral eosinophilia. She was treated with fluocinonide 0.1% ointment twice daily as needed for the rash, which mildly improved. A subsequent biopsy of the left arm was performed approximately 3 months later, showing a subtle interface dermatitis with increased dermal mucin (Figure 2B) and an absence of eosinophils. Retrospectively, a mucin stain was performed of the upper back biopsy, demonstrating an increase in mucin the upper dermis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph from the anti-MDA-5 dermatomyositis case showing the captioned pink, indurated, smooth jawline plaque without epidermal change. The overlying alopecia is described in the text. Although the lesion has tumid lupus-like morphology, the article and caption attribute it to dermatomyositis. B: Patient cheek-biopsy image from the anti-MDA-5 dermatomyositis case showing superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic inflammation in the tumid lupus-like lesion. C: High-power patient cheek-biopsy image showing interface vacuolar alteration, rare necrotic keratinocytes, and superficial lymphocytic inflammation in the lesion reported as tumid lupus-like in anti-MDA-5 dermatomyositis.

in_text_mentions: A 32-year-old man presented with a yearlong history of redness and pain on the lower portion of the right cheek, which was noted to be photosensitive (Fig 1, A). Physical examination was notable for an erythematous, indurated, smooth painful plaque on the lower portion of the right cheek with overlying alopecia. Punch biopsy of the lesion revealed moderately dense superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal predominately lymphocytic infiltrates with limited interface changes, consistent with tumid lupus (Fig 1, B, C). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: The caption explicitly identifies inflammatory infiltrates and necrotic fibers in a muscle biopsy from the dermatomyositis case; perimysial inflammation is represented by the provided histology vocabulary. B: This muscle-biopsy panel directly demonstrates perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation, classic histopathologic manifestations attributed by the caption and disease-focused article to dermatomyositis. C: The caption identifies fibrinoid necrotizing vasculitis in a perimysial vessel from the dermatomyositis patient's biopsy, a recognized less-common histopathologic manifestation of dermatomyositis. D: The same dermatomyositis case biopsy contains a well-formed non-caseating epithelioid granuloma in subcutaneous fat. Granulomatous inflammation is a less-common manifestation of dermatomyositis; no exact finding-key is available.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic findings from the muscle biopsy illustrating inflammatory, granulomatous, and vascular involvement (A) Hematoxylin-eosin staining (HE), low magnification (×100), showing endomysial and perimysial inflammatory infiltrates (white arrows) with scattered necrotic muscle fibers. (B) HE staining, higher magnification (×200) revealing perifascicular muscle fiber atrophy (white arrow) and perivascular inflammation. (C) HE staining of the vascular wall in the perimysium (×400) surrounded by a dense polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate rich in neutrophils, disrupting the vascular basement membrane (white arrow), consistent with necrotizing vasculitis. (D) HE staining, well-formed non-caseating granuloma in subcutaneous adipose tissue (×200) (white arrow), composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: The patient chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities, called interstitial pneumonia in the in-text, within a dermatomyositis/anti-synthetase syndrome case. A specific NSIP, organizing-pneumonia, or rapidly progressive ILD pattern is not stated. B: Bilateral STIR hyperintensity in the vastus lateralis muscles directly demonstrates muscle edema consistent with myositis in the reported dermatomyositis case. C: The muscle H&E section from the reported dermatomyositis patient shows inflammatory-cell infiltration around myofiber bundles, a specific biopsy manifestation of inflammatory myopathy. D: The H&E muscle section visibly demonstrates perivascular inflammatory-cell infiltration, a characteristic histopathologic finding in dermatomyositis. E: CD8 immunohistochemistry demonstrates lymphocyte infiltration in atrophic myofibers, with the in-text localizing the changes to the fascicle periphery, supporting perifascicular atrophy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Patient-derived low-power H&E muscle section with captioned perifascicular atrophy and microinfarction; the in-text biopsy description explicitly links these changes to DM. B: The H&E section shows captioned perifascicular atrophy with necrotic/regenerative fibers and internal nuclei, a characteristic DM myopathy pattern. C: The asterisk marks a captioned focus of microinfarction in the patient's muscle specimen, and the in-text biopsy findings are stated to be consistent with DM. D: The IHC panel demonstrates captioned CD8-positive lymphocytes in endomysial and perimysial tissue, supporting inflammatory DM myopathy. E: The IHC panel demonstrates captioned CD4-positive lymphocytes in endomysial and perimysial tissue, supporting inflammatory DM myopathy. F: The H&E panel is captioned as milder disease involvement with occasional internal nuclei and no rimmed vacuoles; the in-text biopsy description links this patient specimen to DM.
panels.attribution_text: Wu et al. Therapeutic Effects of Treating COVID-19 Vaccine-Induced Anti-TIF1-γ-Positive Dermatomyositis.. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania) 2023. doi:10.3390/medicina59091688. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathology of the muscle biopsy reveals moderate to severe muscle damage. (A) Low-power field showed the muscle tissue with rectangle and asterisk area for perifascicular atrophy and micro infarction. (B) Numerous necrotic/regenerative fibers and internal nuclei fibers are seen. Vague perifascicular atrophy (highlighted by a white arrow) is also noted. (C) A focus of micro infarction is found in the peripheral part of the muscle specimen (asterisk). There are only a few instances of CD8-positive (D) and CD4-positive (E) lymphocyte infiltration in the endomysial myofibers. The lymphocytes are mildly surrounding but not invading the myofibers. Some lymphocytes are also seen in the perimysial areas. (F) Other parts of the muscle showed milder disease involvement, and only occasionally are internal nuclei fibers seen. However, no rimmed vacuoles are seen in the specimen.
in_text_mentions: eps showed muscle tissue with rectangle and asterisk area for perifascicular atrophy and micro infarction, vague perifascicular atrophy, and lymphocyte infiltration in the muscle bundles, which were consistent with the diagnosis of DM (Figure 4). According to the 2017 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) classification criteria for idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), the patient’s score is 11.4 points, surpassing the threshold of 8.7 points. This score supports the classification of the patient as DM (Table 1) [3]. A diagnosis of dermatomyositis post COVID-19 vaccination was suspected.

panels.figure_caption: (a) Violaceous eruptions present around eyelids – heliotrope rash; (b) cutaneous lesions in healing stage
in_text_mentions: On general examination, there was presence of erythematous macular papular lesions over the neck (Figure 1b (Fig. 1)), lower back, extensor surface of arm, shin of tibia and small joints of hands. Neurological examination showed significant wasting and weakness of the proximal muscles of both upper (power=3/5) and lower limbs (power=2/5). Deep tendon reflexes were diminished but sensory examination was within normal limits.

On ophthalmic examination, the patient had heliotrope rashes in the form of violaceous discolouration along with mild swelling over the upper lids of both eyes (Figure 1a (Fig. 1)). The best corrected visual acuity was finger counting close to face (FCCF) in both eyes. Pupillary reactions were sluggish and with no relative apparent pupillary defect (RAPD). Extra-ocular movements were full and there was no subjective complaint of pain on movement.
